SQL Execution Order closes out the SQL Fundamentals module by tying every earlier topic together, revealing the real, internal order clauses actually run in, which genuinely differs from the order you type them in.

This single idea explains nearly every confusing SQL error a beginner runs into, why a column alias cannot be used in WHERE, why HAVING exists separately from WHERE, why LIMIT always applies after sorting. Understanding this real order turns those confusing errors into genuinely predictable, well understood behavior.

1. How This Closes Out the Module
blocks.text: 1. How This Closes Out the Module

blocks.content: Looking back across the module makes the connection clear. SELECT chose which columns. WHERE filtered rows. ORDER BY controlled row order. LIMIT capped row count. DISTINCT removed duplicates. Aliases gave clearer temporary names. Execution order closes the module by explaining how all of these clauses actually run together internally, not just what each one does in isolation.

Every genuinely confusing SQL error covered in earlier topics, a column alias not working in WHERE, being unsure why LIMIT interacts with ORDER BY the way it does, traces directly back to this real execution order, which is why this topic closes the module rather than opening it.

blocks.content: 2. Written Order Versus Executed Order

The order you actually type clauses in a query, SELECT first, then FROM, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT, genuinely does not match the order the database actually executes them in internally.

The real, internal execution order is what genuinely determines a query actual behavior, not the order the words happen to appear on the page. Understanding this real order is what makes several genuinely confusing SQL behaviors suddenly make complete sense.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438303982-539687371.png
3. The Real Order

The genuine internal execution order runs through seven real steps. First, FROM identifies the source tables the query will actually read from. Second, WHERE filters individual rows, before any grouping happens. Third, GROUP BY groups the already filtered rows together. Fourth, HAVING filters those grouped results, specifically based on aggregate values computed per group.

Fifth, SELECT actually chooses and computes the final columns, including any aliases. Sixth, ORDER BY sorts that selected result. And seventh, LIMIT caps the final row count, applied last, after sorting has already genuinely happened.

4. What This Real Order Genuinely Explains
blocks.text: 4. What This Real Order Genuinely Explains

blocks.content: A few real, previously confusing behaviors become genuinely clear once you know this order. Why WHERE cannot use a SELECT column alias, since WHERE runs at step two, and SELECT does not compute that alias until step five, the alias genuinely does not exist yet when WHERE actually runs.

Why HAVING can filter based on aggregate results while WHERE genuinely cannot, since HAVING runs at step four, after GROUP BY has already computed those aggregates, while WHERE runs at step two, before any grouping has happened at all. And why LIMIT always applies after sorting, never before, since LIMIT genuinely runs last, at step seven, well after ORDER BY has already sorted the result at step six.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438309693-220114458.png
blocks.alt: What This Real Order Genuinely Explains

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Trying to filter on an aggregate value, like a count or sum, using WHERE instead of HAVING. WHERE runs before GROUP BY computes those aggregates, so it genuinely has no aggregate value available yet to filter against.
5. A Worked Example
Tracing a real, complete query through this actual execution order makes the whole sequence concrete.

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM employees
WHERE salary>50000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*)>5
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 3;
blocks.code:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM employees
WHERE salary>50000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*)>5
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 3;

codes.sql:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM employees
WHERE salary>50000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*)>5
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 3;

blocks.content: FROM first identifies the employees table. WHERE then filters down to only employees earning above fifty thousand. GROUP BY groups those filtered employees by department. HAVING keeps only departments with more than five employees remaining after that grouping. SELECT then computes the department name and the count, naming that count cnt. ORDER BY sorts departments by that count, highest first. And LIMIT finally keeps only the top three departments from that sorted result.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438309695-121561581.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Once you internalize this real execution order, WHERE versus HAVING, and why aliases work in ORDER BY but not WHERE, stop feeling like arbitrary SQL rules and start feeling like the genuinely logical consequences of this actual sequence.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine query correctness when this execution order is not genuinely understood. Trying to filter on a SELECT column alias inside WHERE, which fails since that alias genuinely does not exist yet at the point WHERE actually runs. Using WHERE to filter an aggregate value instead of HAVING, which fails for the same underlying reason.

And assuming LIMIT happens before ORDER BY sorts the result, which would produce a genuinely different, and usually wrong, set of rows than intended, since LIMIT always applies to the already sorted result, never before sorting happens.
